title: Passover: it would have been enough
hook: a song counting gifts one by one
tomorrow: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, four children, and the one who doesn't know how to ask. Your line was answer each child. Today, a song the whole table shouts.

Partway through the seder, after a long stretch of reading, the energy changes. Someone starts a song with a three-syllable chorus, and suddenly everyone, the uncle checking his phone, the toddler under the table, is shouting it. Day, day, enu. Day, day, enu. In some Persian and Afghan Jewish families, people grab scallions and playfully swat each other during the chorus, recalling the whips of slavery. It can get rowdy. And underneath the noise, the song is doing something careful: counting.
screen: `THE ENERGY CHANGES.` → `SCALLIONS IN THE AIR.` → `UNDERNEATH: COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Dayenu means it would have been enough for us. The song walks through the Exodus in fifteen steps, each one a gift. If God had brought us out of Egypt, and not brought judgment on the Egyptians: dayenu. If God had split the sea, and not led us through on dry ground: dayenu. If God had fed us manna, and not given us Shabbat. If God had brought us to Mount Sinai, and not given us the Torah. All the way to the land of Israel and the Temple. Fifteen times the table shouts: that would have been enough. The Haggadah introduces it with a line: how many good steps God has done for us. The full song appears in an early prayer order compiled in Babylonia by a scholar named Amram Gaon. Some lines sound strange taken literally. Would standing at Sinai without the Torah really have been enough? Teachers have answered in different ways. One answer: the song isn't making a claim about history. It's training the eye. Each step deserved a whole thank-you of its own, so don't let the gifts blur into one lump. Then the Haggadah turns it around: how much more should we be grateful, since God did all of them. It's easy to give thanks in bulk. Dayenu gives thanks one gift at a time.
screen: `FIFTEEN STEPS, FIFTEEN GIFTS.` · `IF ONLY THIS, IT WOULD BE ENOUGH.` · `AN EARLY PRAYER ORDER.` · `HOW MUCH MORE, FOR ALL OF THEM.` · then, large: `IT WOULD HAVE BEEN ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing in your life, maybe a person, and break it into steps: if they had only shown up once, enough; if they had only stayed, enough. Go slowly, one gift at a time, saying dayenu after each, out loud or in your head.
Dayenu. It would have been enough for us: the seder's song of fifteen gifts, counted one by one. Today's word.
Your line: it would have been enough. Fifteen gifts, each one counted on its own. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Why would standing at Sinai without the Torah have been 'enough'? That sounds odd.
options: The song isn't a history claim; it thanks God for each step on its own.
It means Israel never really wanted the Torah, only to leave Egypt.
It's an old copying mistake that teachers quietly skip over.
chat.meaning: One answer teachers give: Dayenu trains the eye, so each gift gets its own thank-you instead of blurring into one lump.
